title: Extracting dipole orientations from asymmetric plasmonic nanostructures towards machine-learning-assisted spectropolarimetry
authors: P. Christian Simo, Michaela Zbytovska, Annika Mildner, Lukas Lang, Melanie Sommer, Dieter P. Kern, Monika Fleischer
abstract: In this work, nanoparticles with various asymmetries are analyzed for their azimuthal orientations using polarimetric dark-field spectroscopy at different analyzing angles of a linear polarizer. This approach reveals their spectral behavior in terms of electric far-field dipole intensities when modeled with an analytical dipole model. By simultaneously fitting the spectra from a set of analyzer angles, the respective dipole orientations are extracted. In a statistical approach, all non-repeating permutations are further studied with a machine learning algorithm. The resulting azimuthal distribution of dipole orientations coincides well with the geometric orientations derived from simulations and electron microscope images. A histogram gradient boosting regressor evaluates the impact of the measurement setup on the simultaneously fitted sets, linking the weights of the analyzer angles to the asymmetry in the plasmonic systems. This comprehensive spectroscopic method improves the accuracy of dipole orientation measurements and enables modern machine learning models to interpret potentially complex features of nanostructures.
summary: This work presents a sophisticated method combining polarimetric dark-field spectroscopy and machine learning to determine the dipole orientations of asymmetric plasmonic nanoparticles. By simultaneously fitting spectral data from multiple polarizer angles, the authors achieve highly accurate orientation measurements. This technique significantly improves the characterization of nanostructure optical properties, linking fundamental physics measurements to advanced computational tools.
main_problem: The paper aims to accurately extract the azimuthal dipole orientations of plasmonic nanostructures from their measured spectral responses.
main_result: The developed machine-learning assisted spectro-polarimetric method successfully extracts dipole orientations that align well with both computational simulations and direct electron microscope measurements.
method: The technique involves polarimetric dark-field spectroscopy, fitting spectra collected at multiple analyzer angles using an analytical dipole model, and employing machine learning (HGBR) for statistical refinement.
model_or_system: The study analyzes asymmetric plasmonic nanoparticles (colloidal and EBL-fabricated) whose localized surface plasmon (LSP) resonances are probed. The analysis is grounded in the Analytical Dipole Model (ADM) and supplemented by multipole decomposition of surface charge densities.
key_observables: Dipole moment orientations ($\gamma_k$), electric far-field dipole intensities, and multipole weights ($	ilde{q}_{\ell m}$).
important_parameters: Analyzer angle ($\Theta$), spectral resonance wavelengths ($\lambda_k$), and the number of simultaneously fitted analyzer angles ($m$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the spectral features can be modeled by the ADM, and that the relative alignment between polarization filters and the sample can be precisely tracked using diffraction patterns.
figures_summary: Figures show SEM images of asymmetric nanoparticles, their dark-field spectra revealing LSP resonances, and simulated surface charge density distributions analyzed via multipole decomposition.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup using polarimetric dark-field spectroscopy, describes the systematic data collection by varying analyzer angles, presents the fitting procedure using the ADM, and validates the results by comparing extracted orientations against simulation and applying ML regression.
why_interesting: While focused on plasmonics, the rigorous combination of advanced optical characterization (spectro-polarimetry) with machine learning for parameter extraction mirrors techniques used in characterizing complex quantum optical systems or analyzing quantum state tomography data.

The total intensity is the sum of the simulated spectra, which is used to normalize the data. The top-down views of the extruded and meshed models are also presented. Their dipole moments are displayed as arrows with their orientation denoted by γk,sim.
